facts: Founded 1878 as Newton Heath LYR F.C. by the Carriage and Wagon department of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway at Newton Heath, Manchester; played in green and gold.
Renamed Manchester United in April 1902 after local brewer John Henry Davies and others rescued the bankrupt Newton Heath; red shirts and white shorts adopted then.

Old Trafford opened on 19 February 1910 (United 3–4 Liverpool); designed by Archibald Leitch; bombed in 1941 and United played at Maine Road until 1949; capacity about 74,000, the largest club ground in Britain; the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand was named in 2011 and the Sir Bobby Charlton Stand in 2016.

Nickname 'the Red Devils': adopted in the early 1960s under Matt Busby, borrowed from Salford rugby league club, which French journalists had called 'Les Diables Rouges' on a 1930s tour; the devil was added to the club crest in the early 1970s. Earlier nicknames were 'the Heathens' (Newton Heath) and 'the Busby Babes' for the young 1950s side.
The club crest is based on the Manchester city coat of arms; the ship on it represents trade and the Manchester Ship Canal.

Munich air disaster, 6 February 1958: the team's aircraft crashed on take-off at Munich-Riem returning from a European Cup tie at Red Star Belgrade; 23 of 44 on board died, including eight players (Geoff Bent, Roger Byrne, Eddie Colman, Duncan Edwards, Mark Jones, David Pegg, Tommy Taylor, Liam Whelan), secretary Walter Crickmer and coaches Tom Curry and Bert Whalley; Matt Busby survived.
First English club to win the European Cup, 1968 (4–1 v Benfica at Wembley, Charlton 2, Best, Kidd), ten years after Munich.

The Treble, 1998–99: Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in one season, the only English men's side to do it; the Champions League final was won 2–1 v Bayern Munich in Barcelona with stoppage-time goals from Sheringham and Solskjær.
Record 20 English league titles; Sir Alex Ferguson managed the club from November 1986 to May 2013 and won 13 of them.
Ownership: the Glazer family bought the club in 2005 in a leveraged takeover; Sir Jim Ratcliffe's INEOS acquired a minority stake in February 2024 and took control of football operations.
Main rivalries: Manchester City (the Manchester derby), Liverpool (the North-West derby) and Leeds United (the Roses rivalry); Arsenal and Chelsea were the great Premier League-era rivals.
Training ground: Carrington (the Trafford Training Centre), opened in 2000, replacing The Cliff in Salford.
Old Trafford's record attendance is 76,962, for an FA Cup semi-final between Wolves and Grimsby in March 1939.
Club anthem associated with the club: 'Glory Glory Man United', released for the 1983 FA Cup final; the Stretford End is the home supporters' end.
